question_text: When measuring a high-side shunt, why is a Difference Amplifier topology an excellent choice compared to a standard Non-Inverting amplifier? How is it wired and what is its equation?
answer_text: A Difference Amplifier explicitly subtracts the two input voltages, amplifying ONLY the difference between them and rejecting the massive common-mode voltage.
explanation_text:
If you used a standard non-inverting amplifier referenced to ground on a 12V rail, the op-amp would try to amplify the massive 12V common-mode voltage, instantly saturating the output.

A Difference Amplifier uses a 4-resistor network (two input resistors, one feedback, one to ground) to actively subtract the inputs.
Equation: V_out = (R_f / R_in) * (V_in+ - V_in-).
If V_in+ is 12.01V and V_in- is 12.00V, it subtracts them and only amplifies the 0.01V difference across the shunt.
bonus_question_text: What is the critical hardware requirement for the 4 resistors in a Difference Amplifier to achieve a good Common-Mode Rejection Ratio (CMRR)?
bonus_answer_text: They must be perfectly matched in highly precise ratios (R1/R2 = R3/R4). Even a 0.1% tolerance mismatch will severely degrade the CMRR, causing the 12V common-mode voltage to artificially leak into the output reading.
